newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon releases study on LatAm training scandal.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon releases study on LatAm training scandal.

text.p: Pentagon investigators on Friday upheld a decision to absolve U.S. officials of blame in the 1980s training of Latin America's military, including support of torture and execution of guerrilla insurgents.

A report by the Defence Department Inspector General's office released by the Pentagon noted that the U.S. Army's School of the Americas had removed "objectionable materials" from its Spanish-language training manuals in 1992.

The report said many mistakes were made in the training from 1982 through 1991, but the Pentagon correctly decided in 1992 not to pursue individual responsibility because there was no evidence of deliberate violation of department policy.

The scandal became public last September with the Pentagon's release of seven Spanish-language U.S. Army manuals used to train Latin American military officers at the School of the Americas over the nine-year period.
The manuals advocated executions, torture, blackmail and other forms of coercion by military intelligence organisations against insurgents.

A Defence Department summary released at the time said manuals suggested that to recruit and control informants, counter-intelligence agents could use "fear, payment of bounties for enemy dead, beatings, false imprisonment, executions and ... truth serum."

The Army School of the Americas, long located in Panama but moved in 1984 to Fort Benning, Georgia, has trained nearly 60,000 military and police officers from Latin America and the United States since 1946.

Former Defence Secretary William Perry asked the inspector general, the department's chief investigator, last year to review a 1992 decision by the department not to pursue individual U.S. responsibility in the scandal.

"The inspector general investigation concludes that the department acted appropriately in 1992 to stop the use of improper materials in training foreign military officers," Deputy Defence Secretary John White said on Friday.
White said that he and new Defence Secretary William Cohen "are committed to doing everyting we can to prevent such mistakes from happening again."
At the suggestion of the inspector general, Assistant Defence Secretary Emmett Paige will review and update an August, 1992 policy memorandum on training foreign military personnel, White said.
Representative Joseph Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, on Friday sharply challenged the conclusion that personnel did not realise the manuals were against standard Defence Department policy.
"These manuals taught tactics that come right out of a Soviet gulag and have no place in civilised society," a statement released by Kennedy said.
